blocks.text: A deque (pronounced "deck") is one of the most flexible data structures you will meet. The name is short for double ended queue, and that name tells you almost everything you need to know.

A normal queue lets you add at one end and remove from the other. A deque removes that restriction. You can add and remove from both ends, the front and the back, and every one of those moves is fast.
Think of a deque as a line of people where someone is allowed to join or leave from either the front or the back at any time.
In this lesson we build a clear mental picture of what a deque is and how it behaves. The next two lessons go deeper into its operations and the problems where it really shines.
A deque is a linear data structure that stores an ordered collection of items and lets you insert or remove elements from both ends in constant time.
Constant time, written O(1), means the work does not grow as the deque gets bigger. Adding to a deque that holds ten items takes the same effort as adding to one that holds ten million.
Because both ends are open, a single deque can behave like several structures at once:

items: Use only one end and it works like a stack (last in, first out)
Add at one end and remove from the other and it works like a queue (first in, first out)
Use both ends freely and you get the full power of a deque

blocks.text: A deque is a superset. Anything a stack or a queue can do, a deque can do too.
Picture a deck of cards resting in your hand. There are only four basic things you can do with it:
Those four moves are the heart of every deque. Let us walk through a small example. We start with an empty deque and apply a few operations, watching the contents change after each step:

codes.python:
from collections import deque

dq = deque()        # []
dq.append(10)       # [10]
dq.append(20)       # [10, 20]
dq.appendleft(5)    # [5, 10, 20]

dq.pop()            # returns 20  ->  [5, 10]
dq.popleft()        # returns 5   ->  [10]

blocks.text: Notice how the front and the back are independent. Touching one end never forces you to shift everything else, and that is exactly why every operation stays O(1).
These three structures are close cousins. The only difference is which ends you are allowed to touch.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Structure","Add at","Remove from","Order"],"rows":[["Stack","One end","Same end","Last in, first out"],["Queue","Back","Front","First in, first out"],["Deque","Front or back","Front or back","Your choice"]]}

blocks.text: If you ever feel limited by a stack or a queue, a deque is usually the upgrade you are looking for.

You almost never build a deque from scratch in an interview. Every major language ships one in its standard library, and it is already fast and well tested. Here is how you create one and use all four core operations:

codes.python:
from collections import deque

dq = deque()

dq.appendleft(5)   # add to the front
dq.append(20)      # add to the back

front = dq[0]      # look at the front
back  = dq[-1]     # look at the back

dq.popleft()       # remove from the front
dq.pop()           # remove from the back

blocks.text: A quick word of advice for each language:

items: Java: prefer ArrayDeque over the older Stack and LinkedList classes. It is faster and cleaner.
Python: use collections.deque. A plain list is slow when you remove from the front.
C++: std::deque gives you push and pop on both ends out of the box.

blocks.text: Reaching for the built in deque saves you time and avoids subtle bugs. Use it.

content.title: 5. Where You Will See a Deque

blocks.text: A deque is the right tool whenever a problem needs fast access to both ends of a sequence. A few common signals to watch for:

items: You need to look at or remove the oldest and the newest item quickly
You are sliding a window across an array and tracking a maximum or a minimum
You are running a breadth first search and want an efficient queue
You want undo and redo style behaviour that works from both ends

blocks.text: The classic interview example is the sliding window maximum problem, where a deque turns a slow solution into a clean linear one. We explore problems like that in the applications lesson.
One line summary: a deque is a queue that is open at both ends, and that small change makes it surprisingly powerful.

description: A gentle introduction to the deque, the double ended queue you can push and pop from both sides.
